items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll use moment-generating functions to prove certain properties about sums of independent random variables with known distributions.

Content:
First, let's introduce some notation:

Content:
> The random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are equal in distribution, written as
> [MATH: X \overset{d}{=} Y]
> if the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are the same for all real values of [MATH: x{:}]
> [MATH: F_X(x) = F_Y(x), \qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R},]
> where [MATH: F_X(x)] and [MATH: F_Y(x)] are the CDFs of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] respectively.

Content:
We're now ready for the main result of this lesson:

Content:
> Let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] be random variables, and [MATH: M_X(t)] and [MATH: M_Y(t)] be the moment-generating functions of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] respectively. If
> [MATH: M_X(t) = M_Y(t)]
> for all values of [MATH: t] in an open interval around [MATH: t=0,] then
> [MATH: X \overset{d}{=} Y.]
> This result is called the uniqueness property of moment-generating functions.

Content:
This means a random variable's probability distribution is uniquely determined by its MGF. Therefore, if the MGF of a random variable matches that of a known distribution, they have the same distribution.

Content:
We can use this result to identify the distributions of sums of independent random variables. Let's see some examples.

For a chi-square random variable [MATH: Y_i \sim \chi^2(k),] we have [MATH: M_{Y_i}(t) = \left(1 - 2t \right)^{-k/2}, \quad t < \dfrac12.]

In our case, since [MATH: Y_{1} \sim \chi^2(2),] we have [MATH: M_{Y_1}(t) = \left(1 - 2t \right)^{-1}, \quad t < \dfrac12.]

sections.normalized_html:
• Sums of Bernoulli Random Variables: Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p)] are independent. Then [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2+ \cdots + X_n \sim B(n,p).] To prove this, let [MATH: M_{X_i}(t)] be the moment-generating function of [MATH: X_i] for [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots, n]. Then, we have [MATH: M_{X_i}(t) = 1 - p + pe^t.] By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions, we have that [MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= M_{X_{1} + X_{2} + ⋯ + X_{n}}(t); = M_{X_{1}}(t) ⋅ M_{X_{2}}(t) ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ M_{X_{n}}(t); = (1 − p + pe^{t}) ⋅ (1 − p + pe^{t}) ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ (1 − p + pe^{t}); = (1 − p + pe^{t})^{n},] which is the moment-generating function of a binomial random variable with distribution [MATH: B(n, p).]

    Now, since any given distribution is characterized by its moment-generating function (meaning that no other distribution can have the same moment-generating function), we conclude that [MATH: Y\sim B(n,p).]

  • Sums of Binomial Random Variables: Suppose [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p)] are independent. Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll use moment-generating functions to prove certain properties about sums of independent random variables with known distributions.

Content:
First, let's introduce some notation:

Content:
> The random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are equal in distribution, written as
> [MATH: X \overset{d}{=} Y]
> if the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are the same for all real values of [MATH: x{:}]
> [MATH: F_X(x) = F_Y(x), \qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R},]
> where [MATH: F_X(x)] and [MATH: F_Y(x)] are the CDFs of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] respectively.

Content:
We're now ready for the main result of this lesson:

Content:
> Let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] be random variables, and [MATH: M_X(t)] and [MATH: M_Y(t)] be the moment-generating functions of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] respectively. If
> [MATH: M_X(t) = M_Y(t)]
> for all values of [MATH: t] in an open interval around [MATH: t=0,] then
> [MATH: X \overset{d}{=} Y.]
> This result is called the uniqueness property of moment-generating functions.

Content:
This means a random variable's probability distribution is uniquely determined by its MGF. Therefore, if the MGF of a random variable matches that of a known distribution, they have the same distribution.

Content:
We can use this result to identify the distributions of sums of independent random variables. Let's see some examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Distribution of a Sum of Discrete Random Variables

Example Prompt:
Consider the independent random variables [MATH: Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_{10}] where [MATH: Y_i\sim \mathrm{B}(5,0.3)] for [MATH: 1\leq i \leq 10.] What is the distribution of [MATH: Y=Y_1+Y_2+\cdots + Y_{10}?]

Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results.

| Distribution | [MATH: M(t)] | [MATH: t]-domain |
| [MATH: U \{ x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n} \left( e^{x_1t} + e^{x_2t} + \ldots + e^{x_nt} \right)] | [MATH: t\in\mathbb R] |
| [MATH: \textrm{Bernoulli}(p)] | [MATH: 1-p+pe^t] | [MATH: t\in\mathbb R] |
| [MATH: B(n,p)] | [MATH: (1-p+pe^t)^n] | [MATH: t\in\mathbb R] |
| [MATH: \textrm{Geom}(p)] | [MATH: \dfrac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}] | [MATH: t<-\ln (1-p)] |
| [MATH: \textrm{NB}(n,p)] | [MATH: \left(\dfrac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}\right)^n] | [MATH: t<-\ln (1-p)] |
| [MATH: \text{Po}(\lambda)] | [MATH: e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}] | [MATH: t\in\mathbb R] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a random variable's probability distribution is uniquely determined by its moment-generating function (MGF). Therefore, if the MGF of a random variable [MATH: X] matches that of a known distribution, then [MATH: X] has the same distribution.

For a binomial random variable [MATH: Y_i \sim \textrm{B}(n,p),] we have
[MATH: M_{Y_i}(t) = (1-p+pe^t)^n.]

In our case, since [MATH: Y_i \sim \textrm{B}(5,0.3),] we have
[MATH: M_{Y_{i}}(t)|= (1 − 0.3 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}; = (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}.]

If [MATH: Y = Y_1+Y_2+\cdots + Y_{10},] where [MATH: Y_1, Y_2,\ldots Y_{10}] are independent random variables with moment-generating function [MATH: M_{Y_i}(t),] then the moment-generating function of [MATH: Y] is

[MATH: M_Y(t) = M_{Y_1}(t) \cdot M_{Y_2}(t) \cdots M_{Y_{10}}(t)]

In our case, we have
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5} ⋅ (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}⋯(0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{5}^(⏞)^(10times); = (0.7 + 0.3e^{t})^{50}.]

Notice that [MATH: M_Y(t)] is the MGF of a binomial random variable with [MATH: n = 50] and [MATH: p= 0.3.]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: Y\sim B(50,0.3).]

[MATH: M_{X_i}(t) = 1 - p + pe^t.]
By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions, we have that
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= M_{X_{1} + X_{2} + ⋯ + X_{n}}(t); = M_{X_{1}}(t) ⋅ M_{X_{2}}(t) ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ M_{X_{n}}(t); = (1 − p + pe^{t}) ⋅ (1 − p + pe^{t}) ⋅ ⋯ ⋅ (1 − p + pe^{t}); = (1 − p + pe^{t})^{n},]
which is the moment-generating function of a binomial random variable with distribution [MATH: B(n, p).]

Now, since any given distribution is characterized by its moment-generating function (meaning that no other distribution can have the same moment-generating function), we conclude that
[MATH: Y\sim B(n,p).]
- Sums of Binomial Random Variables: Suppose [MATH: X_1\sim B(n_1,p)] and [MATH: X_2\sim B(n_2,p)] are independent. Then
